pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, 'showing your working' is the first rung of mathematical argument: the child shows and tells HOW an answer was found — with objects, a drawing, or spoken words — and begins to respond to 'how do you know?' by pointing to what they did rather than just restating the answer. On the NRICH novice-to-expert ladder this is the describing (and beginning-to-explain) stage. The crucial teaching insight is that at this age a child's REASONING typically runs ahead of their ability to COMMUNICATE it: a child who says little may nonetheless have reasoned soundly. So teaching separates the two — building the habit of demonstrating a method concretely, and, separately, scaffolding the language to narrate it — and treats listening to a peer and agreeing/disagreeing as the seed of critiquing reasoning.
bestPractices: Ask 'how do you know?' and 'show me' routinely, accepting objects, pointing, and drawings as valid ways to show working
Separate reasoning from its communication — judge whether a quiet child needs help thinking or help putting it into words, and support each differently
Model narrating a method aloud ('first I… then I…') and provide simple spoken stems
Use concrete referents (counters, ten frames, drawings) as the medium of explanation, as elementary arguments legitimately rest on objects and actions
Have children listen to a peer's method and say whether they agree, beginning to evaluate reasoning rather than just answers
Value the demonstration itself; do not treat limited vocabulary as limited mathematics
keyRepresentations: Concrete objects / counters moved to enact and show a method
The describe → explain step of the NRICH reasoning ladder
commonMisconceptions: Restating the answer ('because it's 8') when asked 'how do you know?' instead of showing the method
A quiet or brief response mistaken for weak reasoning, when it is really communication that lags
Judging a peer's work only by whether the answer matches, not by whether the method makes sense
Believing 'showing your working' means writing the sum again rather than revealing the thinking

learn.summary: For 5-6 year olds, 'showing your working' means demonstrating and narrating HOW an answer was found — with objects, drawings, or spoken words — and beginning to answer 'how do you know?' by pointing to what was done rather than restating the answer. A key teaching insight is that at this age reasoning can often run ahead of the ability to communicate it: a quiet child may have reasoned soundly. Teaching therefore separates two threads — building the habit of demonstrating a method concretely, and separately scaffolding the language to narrate it — and treats listening to a peer and agreeing/disagreeing as the first seed of evaluating reasoning, not just answers.

activities.title: The curious listener who wants to know HOW
feedback: When the child shows and narrates a method, reflect it back as a short story so they hear their own doing turned into an explanation.
Accept spoken, pointed, tapped, or dragged responses, and never penalise sparse words — value the demonstration itself.
If the child only restates '8' or 'because it's right', prompt 'show me with your counters' and 'point to where the 3 went'.
When presenting a muddled-but-correct route, help the child attend to the steps rather than accept it just because the answer matched; make clear the muddled route is not the model to copy.
activities.rationale: Showing and telling how you worked something out is inherently dialogic. A character that keeps asking 'how do you know? show me!' and genuinely listens — accepting objects and pointing — rehearses the describe/explain habit and gives the child a reason to narrate a method aloud, which is where communication of reasoning is built. A deliberately wrong-but-plausible worked route plants the first seed of judging reasoning rather than answers. These are research-informed design proposals, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents (objects, drawings, diagrams, actions), and students at all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask questions to improve them.

Reasoning develops along a describe → explain → convince → justify → prove spectrum; the reasoning itself and the communication of it are distinct and often develop at different rates, with young children's reasoning frequently ahead of their ability to communicate it.
learnerActions: Solve a within-10 problem such as 5 and 3 using counters (physical objects or on-screen draggable counters).
When asked 'how did you get 8? show me!', move or point to the counters to re-enact the method — for example, 'I put 5, then counted on 3 more'.
Hear the method echoed back as a little story ('first you put 5, then you counted on 3 more, so you got 8') and notice that explaining = showing the doing, not repeating the answer.
Watch the listener solve a problem its own way — sometimes by a muddled or wrong route — and answer 'do you agree with how I did it? how can you tell?'
activities.intendedInsight: 'How do you know?' is answered by demonstrating the method, not by restating the answer; and a method can be judged by whether its steps make sense, not only by whether the final number is right.

activities.title: Show-how workspace with a compare-two-methods panel
feedback: Prompt the child to narrate alongside the replay so the demonstration and its words are built together.
On the compare panel, ask the child to point to the specific step they agree or disagree with rather than give a yes/no.
Treat a correct answer reached by an odd route as a chance to notice the method, not to approve it automatically.
activities.rationale: A workspace where the child moves counters or ten-frames to show a method and then narrates it makes the demonstration concrete and repeatable; a simple 'do you agree?' comparison introduces evaluating reasoning. Draggable counters, a replay of the steps, and a side-by-side compare panel are illustrative interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms, and are not validated here.
sourceClaims: Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents (objects, drawings, diagrams, actions), and students at all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask questions to improve them.
learnerActions: Move counters or fill a ten frame to solve an addition or subtraction, then use a 'show how you did it' replay to retrace the steps.
Narrate the recaptured steps aloud using stems such as 'first… then… so…'.
View a peer's or character's method beside your own and decide 'do you agree?', then 'show why' by pointing to a step that does or does not make sense.
activities.intendedInsight: A method can be made concrete, repeatable, and comparable; evaluating reasoning means looking at the steps, not only matching the final answer.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal a worked method (modelling scaffold)
feedback: Use the revealed stages as a model, then quickly move the child to demonstrating their own method so they do not only watch.
Name each revealed step in 'first… then… so…' form so the language of narration is modelled.
activities.rationale: Revealing a worked method's steps one at a time can model what showing your working looks like, but the child watches rather than demonstrates their own thinking, so it should lead into own-method demonstration. Recognition of a modelled method does not by itself elicit the child producing and narrating one. This is a modelling scaffold whose effectiveness is untested by the cited sources, not a substitute for the child producing and narrating a method.
learnerActions: Tap each stage of an already-solved problem to reveal 'what I did and why' at that step.
Afterwards, re-solve a fresh problem and show your own steps with objects or a drawing, narrating as you go.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the stages of a worked method named out loud shows what 'showing your working' can look like before producing one's own.

constraints: The target is demonstrating AND beginning to evaluate a method — not producing a single scored answer. An answer-only, scored format can record only the final result and cannot capture showing or telling a method, and it tends to reward the answer-restating this topic must move beyond; if used at all, treat it as a check of the final result, not of the reasoning.
A tap-to-reveal worked example is a modelling scaffold: the child watches rather than demonstrates, so it must be followed by the child producing and narrating their own method.

Separate reasoning from its communication: when a child is quiet or brief, judge whether they need help thinking or help putting it into words, and support that thread. Do not treat limited vocabulary as limited mathematics, and do not drill vocabulary in isolation.
Elementary arguments legitimately rest on objects, pointing, and drawings; accept these as valid ways to show working rather than requiring written sums or rich sentences.
At this age, full critique of a peer's reasoning is only emerging; expect the child to begin attending to steps (e.g. 'can you show what I did?') rather than deliver a complete evaluation.

Showing arithmetic working here does not need elaborate 3D spatial environments: simple concrete arrangements such as counters and ten frames are useful for showing a method, but complex spatial/3D manipulation is not needed for this objective, though it may serve other topics.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified in this independent review, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit of every summary, insight, action, feedback, constraint and note found no new critical learner-facing errors or unsupported categorical claims; the previously flagged activities[2].sourceClaims=[] correction is confirmed already applied.

The included diagnostic routine (solve 5+3 with counters, ask 'how do you know? show me', then model an alternative or deliberately slipped method and ask 'do you agree?') is arithmetically sound: 5+3=8. No numeric errors were found in the source examples.

A deliberately 'wrong way' demonstration by the character should remain clearly a muddled route to test the child's attention to steps; ensure any wrong demonstration is not left as the child's takeaway model of correct method.

The tap-to-reveal activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because neither cited claim directly supports the efficacy of a watch-first modelling scaffold; the claims concern reasoning development generally, not evidence that this interaction helps.

The original source framed an answer-only scored format and a 3D/spatial format as 'poor fit'; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal 'cannot teach' claims.

probeDeeper: 'Show me with the counters how you got 8.' (turns 'how do you know?' into a demonstration)
'Can you tell me the first thing you did, and the next thing?' (scaffolds narrating the method)
'I'll do it my way — watch. Do you agree with how I did it?' (evaluating a method, not an answer)
Counterexample: solve it by a muddled route that still lands on 8 — does the child notice the method was odd, or accept it because the answer is right?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who responds to 'how do you know?' by SHOWING the method (moving or pointing to counters, or drawing) and telling it in some form ('I had 5, then 3 more'), and who, watching your method, judges it by whether the actions make sense rather than only whether the answer matches. Demonstrating the method and beginning to evaluate a method are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reasoning runs ahead of communication — the child clearly used a sound method but 'just tells the answer' or cannot yet put the how into words.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT conclude the child cannot reason, and do not drill vocabulary in isolation. Ask them to SHOW with counters and narrate alongside; decide whether it is the reasoning or the communication that needs developing, and support that one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'how do you know?', the child gives the correct answer and a shrug or a single word, yet can correctly re-do the problem when watched — the thinking is there, the language is not.

errorPatterns.pattern: Restates the answer when asked 'how do you know?' ('because it's 8') instead of showing the method.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the move explicitly: 'show me with your counters', 'point to where the 3 went'; model narrating a method so the child hears what 'how' sounds like.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child repeats the result rather than demonstrating; the show-and-tell habit is not yet triggered by the prompt.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges a peer's (or teacher's) method only by whether the answer matches, not by whether the steps make sense.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not expect full critique yet; ask 'can you show what I did?' so the child attends to the steps, and use agree/disagree talk with clear listening turns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown a method that reaches the right answer by a muddled route, the child agrees simply because the answer is right; evaluating the reasoning itself is only emerging.

responseLevels.gap: Gives only the answer or 'because it's right'; cannot show the method even with objects; judges others solely by the answer.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously demonstrates the method with objects/drawing and narrates it in some form, and when watching another method attends to whether the steps make sense — the seed of critiquing reasoning — not just the answer.
responseLevels.partial: Shows and describes WHAT they did with objects or a drawing (the describing step), but not yet WHY, and needs prompting; begins to look at a peer's steps only when asked.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child counters and a problem like 5 + 3. Once they have 8, ask: 'How do you know it's 8? Show me and tell me how you worked it out.' Then solve it yourself a different way (or with a deliberate slip), and ask: 'Do you agree with how I did it? How can you tell?' Treat it as a conversation about their thinking, not a marked answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child developing this practice turns 'how do you know?' into a demonstration — they re-enact the doing. A child at answer-only restates '8' or 'because it's right' and, when judging your method, checks only the final number. Because a young child's words may lag their thinking, the tell is whether they can SHOW the method (with objects) even when they cannot fully narrate it — not the richness of their vocabulary.
